name: Dana Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We own Hazel Bank, 70 hectares, with 200 dairy goats and barley on the flatter fields. Milking's at six, then I'm in the cheese room most of the morning making our hard goat's cheese. Afternoons are the farm shop and the online orders, which an AI assistant mostly sorts now, it answers customers and books the courier. My husband Ray drives a lorry three days a week and does the barley the rest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the cheese. Twenty years in and I still get excited cutting a new wheel. What wears me out is the milking twice a day, every day, no exceptions. I'm 58 and my wrists know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful assistant and leave it at that. I'd probably post on the cheesemakers' forum that it saves me about six hours a week on orders, which is true. Hype aside, that's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means Hazel Bank carries on doing well. We've got good savings, the land's ours and the cheese sells. I'm comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the AI assistant on the orders and try it on the cheese room records, the temperature logs. Keep milking, keep making cheese. Maybe look at a second-hand milking robot in a few years to save my wrists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with the six hours you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The six hours go on the cheese, honestly. Last winter I used the six hours AI saved me to try a washed-rind cheese, and it's now our second-best seller. That's what the time's for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anyone in the family who'd see it differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Kasia's a graphic designer in the city, and AI has already cut her work a bit. In AI Plateau she'd keep most of it, so I'd tell her to hang on. Our son Adam's a nurse abroad, so he's fine either way.

It saves me about **six hours** a week on orders, which is real.
think: With savings, **our own land** and steady cheese sales, I'm comfortable.
Nothing in this picture **threatens** our living.
do: Use the AI for the **temperature logs** as well as orders.
Keep **milking** and making cheese as now.
Look at a **second-hand milking robot** in a few years.

steps.text: Put the cheese room temperature logs on the AI assistant
Keep milking 200 goats and making the hard cheese

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms that sell direct should grab it with both hands. It does the boring parts of running a shop, the emails, the stock, the bookings. I'd run a session at the cheesemakers' meeting on how I set mine up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly good. The thinking side of Hazel Bank is the shop and the orders, and AI already does a lot of that. The milking and the cheese change slowly, and that hands-on part is what customers pay for anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let AI take the whole online shop, stock, pricing and customer emails, within six months. I'd spend about 25,000 extending the cheese room so I can make more with the time I get back. And I'd talk Ray into using an AI planner for his barley, because he still does it on the back of an envelope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the first warm day in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ray go along with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray would grumble but he'd use it. He's slower to pick these things up but he's not stubborn. He'll try anything once if I set it up for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in this picture a worry for the household's money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray's lorry work might go in the end, but the card says robots are slow, and he only does three days a week. It's pocket money for him, really, not the household income. So no, I'm not worried about money.

Doesn't count **Ray's lorry wage** as a household risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast, and people need help, but there's no point pretending it isn't happening. I'd tell other small producers to get their own AI working now. I'd also say government should help the ones who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Hazel Bank, the AI in 2028 is just more of what I've got. The robots in 2031 are the question: if a factory robot can make a goat's cheese as good as mine, the price falls. I think people will still pay for a farm cheese made by a person, but I'm not certain, and that's the bit I'd chew on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd put about 90,000 into a milking robot, which saves my wrists whatever happens. From 2028 I'd let AI run all the selling and the paperwork. And I'd start cheesemaking courses on the farm, maybe 150 a head, because the one thing a robot can't sell is an afternoon with the person who makes the cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy. I'm betting on people wanting a real person, and I could be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the family would be hit hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia. Design work would be gone by 2028, I'd think. I'd tell my daughter Kasia she can come and run the courses and the farm's brand with me, if she wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ray's driving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray's lorry would probably go with the robots around 2031. He's 60 then, so he'd just stop, and that's fine, he'd been talking about it. He'd do the barley and help with the courses.

Small producers should get **their own AI** working now.
think: The **AI in 2028** is just more of what I already use.
**Robot-made cheese** from 2031 could push my prices down.

fieldNote: The **gap to 2031** gives her time to build a human-made selling point.
Already plans a **milking robot**, mainly to save her wrists.
Offers a place on the farm to her daughter **Kasia**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run-up, and farms that plan will be fine. I'd keep sharing what works on the cheesemakers' forum. Honestly, I'd enjoy being useful to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a comfortable timeline. AGI in 2031, robots in 2034 when I'm 66. I'd have the milking robot paid off and the courses running long before either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the milking robot in the next two years, while the price drops. I'd build the courses up slowly and test them for a couple of years. And I'd try every new AI tool that comes out for small food businesses, because that's what I do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to find out first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd want to know is how the robot cheese tastes. I'd buy one the first week and do a blind tasting with my regulars. If they can't tell, I'd need to think harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if your regulars can't tell the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lean even more on the farm visits, the goats, the story. People don't drive forty minutes to a farm for a cheese, they drive for the day out. A robot can't give anyone a day out on a goat farm.

say: I'd keep sharing **what works** on the cheesemakers' forum.
I'd **enjoy** being useful to other small producers.
think: The **timeline** suits me: robots around 2034, when I'm 66.
The **milking robot** and courses would be running long before.
do: Buy the **milking robot** within two years as prices drop.
Build and **test the courses** for a couple of years.
Try every new **AI tool** for small food businesses.
S3.quote: People don't drive forty minutes to a farm for a cheese, they drive for the day out.
fieldNote: Plans a **blind tasting** against robot cheese, a very hands-on test.

steps.text: Buy the milking robot within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, and there's no excuse not to be ready. I'd say it kindly, though. Not everyone's as keen on gadgets as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's after I've wound down. I'd be 68 when AGI arrives and 71 for the robots. Kasia or someone else would be running the cheese by then, if anyone is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: milking robot within a few years, courses, AI on the shop. I'd start talking with Kasia and Adam about whether either of them wants Hazel Bank. If not, I'd plan to sell to a young cheesemaker around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to happen to Hazel Bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want it to stay a cheese farm. I'd sell Hazel Bank for a bit less to someone who'd keep the goats going rather than to whoever offers most. That's my one soft spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retirement look like for you and Ray?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray would be fully retired, and he'd want to go fishing. I'd want to keep making one cheese a week until my hands give out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, I suppose, but more for Kasia than for me. The farm would cope. What would help is for small producers to get cheap, simple AI tools and training, and for younger people like my daughter to get help moving into new work fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask if anything here is good news. For me a lot of it is. Getting the screen work off my plate gave me back the cheese, and the cheese is why I started farming.
